Description: This type of feedback is usually generated based on pre-trained models. This mechanism consists of three crucial components:  output, feedback, and refinement. Firstly, the agent  generates an output. Then, it utilizes LLMs to provide feedback on the output and offers guidance on how to refine it. At last, the output is improved by the feedback and refinement. This output-feedback-refinement process iterates until reaching some desired conditions.
Motivation: An agent generates a plan regarding the users' goals and requirements and then decomposes the goals into a set of tasks for achieving goals. But the issue that arises is that the generated plan might be affected from hallucinations of the Foundation Model - Another question that arises is how to review the plan and reasoning steps and incorporate feedback efficiently in this process.
Solution: User prompts specific goals to the agent which then generates a plan to accomplish users' requirements. The user can instruct the agent to reflect on the plan and the corresponding reasoning process. Agent will backtrack inference process to verify the intermediate results and adjust the reasoning process accordingly. (process can be saved in agent's memory for continuous learning)

Description: This type of reflection pattern uses different agents or Foundation Models to provide feedback and refinements on the plan.
Alias: Peer Review Pattern [3], Reflect & Critique Pattern [4], Evaluator Optimiser Pattern [6]
Category: Reflection Pattern [1][2][5], Interaction Pattern [3], Workflow Pattern [4][6]
Motivation: When an agent has limited capability to conduct reflection with satisfying performance, the question is how can the output and the reasoning steps of this agent be evaluated. The inconsistencies of an agent's reasoning process may reduce response accuracy and the trustworthiness of the agent might be disturbed by the issue of transparency in plan generation. Lastly, an agent might not be able to perfom reflection due to its limited capability.
Solution: If an agent cannot generate accurate results or precise planning steps via reflecting its outputs, users can prompt it to query another agent which is specialised in reflection - so the latter will review and evaluate the logged outputs and relevant reasoning steps of the 1st agent and provide suggestions.

Description: The agents are empowered with the capability  to call external tools for executing action.
Motivation: Even if LLMs have been demonstrated to be effective in accomplishing a large amount of tasks, they may not work well for the domains which need comprehensive expert  knowledge or they might also encounter  hallucination problems, which are hard to be resolved by themselves.
Solution: For these reason the foundation models might utilize external tools like API calls, databases and knowledge bases or  external models that will alleviate hallucination issues or issues that have to do with limited domain knowledge.

Description: In addition to utilizing  external tools, many agents rely solely on the internal knowledge of LLMs to guide their actions and decisions.
Motivation: For simplicity and fast implementation, agents cannot always depend on external tools or APIs for reasoning, planning, or interaction.
Solution: The solution is for an agentic system to utilize its internal knowledge (as they are already pretrained on large amount of data).

Description: Single-modality agents utilize one type of input such as text, vision, or audio which makes them ideal for straightforward tasks that require less computational resources and simpler data interpretation.
Motivation: Need for a straightforward task optimization of a single modality type (audio, text, vision) with less computational resources.
Solution: Single-modality agents utilize one type of input such as text, vision, or audio that has simple data processing and interpretation processes.

Description: In contrast, multi-modality agents combine video/audio/image/text inputs uploaded by humans, and understand the operational and environmental context, enabling a more comprehensive and rich interaction with their environment.
Motivation: From nature, single modality agents are limited in their ability to capture the richness of real world contexts. The need for agentic systems is to be able to act in multimodal environments involving language, vision, sound, and situational cues.
Solution: Development of multi-modal agents that integrate and reason across diverse input types. By combining modalities, agents can interpret environmental signals, align perception with user commands, and respond in contextually appropriate ways.

Description: Only one model is used. A single-model agent handles all tasks, which makes it suitable for simpler systems with a limited scope. This approach minimizes complexity but may not scale well for diverse tasks.
Motivation: Need for simpler systems, with a simple task to perform, limited needs and also minimal complexity.
Solution: Utilization of only a single model agent for fast implementation when a small scope and simple task is needed to be performed.

Description: Here, multiple models are used in the same agent. In more complex systems, multi-model configurations are often employed. Multiple models are used to handle different tasks or to enhance performance.
Motivation: A single model often struggles to balance efficiency, specialization, and scalability across diverse tasks, because complex systems require handling varied workloads (ome demanding domain expertise, others requiring efficiency or robustness).
Solution: Adoption of a multi model configuration, where different models are integrated to perform complementary to one another functions.

Description: Short-term memory handles short-term information relevant to immediate tasks. This type of memory is useful for temporary activities that do not require long-term storage, for example, configuration, working context, recent events, and the information within the context window of the Foundation Model.
Motivation: Agents often need to access and use information that is only relevant to the current task or interaction. Storing such details in long term memory would be inefficient and unnecessary.
Solution: Implementation of a short term memory component that temporarily stores relevant to the task information within the agent�s working context. This includes configuration details, recent actions and any piece of information that fits within the Foundation Model�s context window.

Description: Long-term memory retains information over long periods of time, which is essential for tasks that require historical data, knowledge, past observations and experiences.
Motivation: Many agent tasks require continuity and learning from past experiences.
Solution: Integration of a long term memory component that stores information such as historical data and prior observations. This allows agents to recall past events, build context across sessions, and continuously refine their behavior based on experience.

Description: This pattern enables agents to get rid of irrelevant or outdated information, making sure that they maintain optimal performance without being burdened by unnecessary data. This capability is crucial in dynamic environments where data can be quickly considered relevant or irrelevant
Motivation: In dynamic environments, agents constantly encounter new information, much of which becomes irrelevant or outdated over time. Retaining all data not only wastes resources but also clutters decision-making, slowing down responses and reducing effectiveness.
Solution: Implementation of selective forgetting mechanisms that allow agents to identify and discard irrelevant or outdated information.

Description: Memory  information like the agents' observations and outputs are and using natural language. In that way the memory information can be expressed  in a flexible way, by keeping rich semantic information that can provide  comprehensive information able to guide agent behaviors.
Motivation: Agentic AI systems need a memory format that is both flexible and semantically rich to capture experiences, observations, and behaviors. Traditional symbolic or structured representations can be rigid and may fail to preserve nuanced context.
Solution: Using natural language as the representation format for storing memory. By encoding experiences, feedback, and skills directly in raw text, agents can retain semantic richness, maintain interpretability, and flexibly adapt memory to diverse contexts.

Description: Memory reflection allows agents to summarize and infer high-level insights from their past experiences and interractions, making abstract and complex decision-making possible.
Motivation: Need for retrieval of information from past agent interactions and responses.
Solution: Retrieval of information from past interactions in order for repetition of parameters that led to successful task completions to become apparent.

Description: Able to transform memory information into compact embedding vectors proved to enhance the efficiency of memory retrieval processes.
Motivation: Need for enhancement of retrieval and reading efficiency.
Solution: Embeddings have been proven to be an efficient way of retrival for all types of data.

Description: Databases enable precise memory operations through SQL queries, providing structured and efficient data management.
Motivation: Foundation models alone cannot reliably store or retrieve detailed, up to date, or domain-specific knowledge. They need access to external databases or knowledge bases.
Solution: Integrating  external databases or knowledge bases enables agents  to obtain specific domain information for generating  more realistic actions.

Description: In that format information is systematically organized in lists or hierarchical structures that clearly showcase the relationships between the elements and allow fast data access and retrieval.
Motivation: Need for structured representations, in this case lists, that represent hierarchical data information and relationships that enable agents to efficiently navigate the relationships between elements, improving the speed and accuracy of access and retrieval.
Solution: Organization of information in systematic structures like lists that explicitly capture relationships between elements.

Description: Here, agents in the coordinator role formulate highlevel strategies and orchestrate the execution of tasks by delegating task execution responsibilities to other agents, external tools, or non-agent systems so that tasks are delegated efficiently.
Motivation: In multi-agent or hybrid systems, someone must keep track of the bigger picture. Without a coordinating role, agents risk working at cross-purposes, duplicating efforts, or leaving gaps in execution.
Solution: Assigning agents the role of setting high-level strategies, breaking down goals, and orchestrating workflows.

Description: Here, agents in the worker role need to generate strategies and execute specific tasks in line with those strategies.
Motivation: High-level strategies alone are not enough. Systems need agents that can actually perform concrete tasks. Without worker agents, plans remain abstract and never translate into real action.
Solution: Designing agents to focus on carrying out specific strategies or sub-tasks. Worker agents handle concrete execution, applying domain knowledge or specialized skills to achieve the objectives defined by the coordinator.

Description: Involves a central agent or system managing the coordination of all agents. This approach provides strong oversight but can become a bottleneck, particularly in large-scale system.
Category: Coordination-Cooperation Pattern, Workflow Pattern, Architecture Pattern
Motivation: When task management is fragmented across many agents, the system risks inconsistency, duplication, or conflict.
Solution: A centralized control point that ensures uniform procedures, predictable outcomes, and easier oversight, especially in environments where consistency and compliance are important.

Description: Federated coordination is managed in a decentralized manner, with each agent handling its own coordination while still communicating with others.
Category: Coordination-Cooperation Pattern, Workflow Pattern, Architecture Pattern
Motivation: Over-reliance on a single control point can create bottlenecks and a single point of failure.
Solution: Distribution of task management responsibilities across multiple agents. Each agent executes and manages tasks semi-independently, coordinating with others as needed.

Description: This pattern involves no central coordinator, as all agents coordinate directly with each other, often using peer-to-peer communication protocols.
Category: Coordination-Cooperation Pattern, Workflow Pattern, Architecture Pattern
Motivation: Need of automatization of agent coordination based on the agentic system's needs.
Solution: Adopting a non-central coordination, where agents utilize peer to peer coordination directly deciding themselves the delegation of intermediate tasks and processes.

Description: In this pattern, all information is openly shared among agents. This maximizes cooperation and ensures that all agents have the same level of information, which can be particularly beneficial in collaborative environments.
Motivation: In collaborative multi-agent environments, uneven access to information can cause inefficiency, misalignment, or duplicated effort.
Solution: Adopting a full transparency strategy, where all relevant information is openly shared among agents. This guarantees equal access to knowledge, enabling agents to build on each other�s findings and coordinate effectively in complex tasks.

Description: Information between the agents in a system is shared only if it is relevant to achieving specific goals.
Motivation: Not all types of shared information might be of importance to the agents for achieving the goal.
Solution: Adopting a strategy where information of the intermediate steps and processes will be shared only if they are important to the final goal - avoiding overloading the agents with unneeded information.

Description: Information is shared based on the roles, individual tasks and responsibilities of each agent.
Motivation: The need for agents to share information with each other based on their individual roles, because this will assist with the understanding and importance of their related outputs and point of view.
Solution: Adopting a strategy of sharing each agent's roles that helps with the aknoledgement of agent importance and better inter agent response and output.

Description: Sensitive information is withheld to protect privacy and security. This approach is crucial in scenarios where data sensitivity is high, and privacy regulations must be strictly followed.
Motivation: The need for preserving sensitive data when dealing with sensitive types of information that should be anonymized or kept secret.
Solution: Adopting methods to protect sensitive data for security and privacy reasons.

Description: Information sharing is adapted based on the context and current state of the system.
Motivation: Unrestricted information sharing can overwhelm agents, while overly restrictive sharing may deprive them of critical knowledge. In dynamic environments, agents need to balance efficiency, privacy, and relevance.
Solution: Implementing context-aware sharing mechanisms where agents tailor the information they exchange based on both intrinsic context (for example their goals, history, internal state) and extrinsic context (for example user preferences, other agents� behaviors, systemic norms).

Description: The Chain of Thought (CoT) mechanism involves the agent articulating its reasoning process step-by-step, mirroring human cognitive processes. This method helps in tracing how decisions are made and identifying where errors might have occurred.
Category: Reflection Pattern [1], Cognitive Pattern [2], Explainability & Transparency Pattern [3]
Motivation: Linear answers make it hard to validate decisions or learn from mistakes. Complex tasks benefit from exposing intermediate assumptions and check so errors can be spotted early and reasoning can be assisted.
Solution: Having the agent articulate its reasoning as ordered steps. Also using internals that structure a step by step decomposition and self-verification, logging intermediate states for validation and iterative improvement.

Description: Tree of Thoughts (ToT) extends the reflection process by allowing agents to explore multiple reasoning pathways simultaneously. This mechanism helps agents to consider various possible outcomes before settling on a final decision, enhancing the robustness and depth of the decision-making process.
Motivation: Single-path reasoning can miss alternatives. For ambiguous, multi-step problems, exploring only one chain reduces robustness and final quality.
Solution: Having the agent branch into multiple candidate reasoning paths.

Description: This pattern analyses users� articulated goals through the dialogue interface.
Motivation: The need to support users who may lack expertise in interaction with agentic systems or LLMs and assist them in clarifying their goals sufficiently. Bridging the gap between underspecified user input & actionable agent objectives.
Solution: Enabling the foundation model based agent to interpret user context and problems via dialogue interface. The LLM agent passively receives these inputs and enhances them by retrieving relevant info from memory.

Description: Proactive goal creator anticipates users� goals by understanding human interactions and capturing the context via relevant tools.
Motivation: The need to overcome the limitations of passive, text based input by enabling the agent to actively capture, interpret and enrich content from the user's environment. (incomplete, ambiguous, inaccessible user input)
Solution: Enhancing agent goal determination by actively capturing multimodal contextual information - beyond info and memory. Sending the requirements to external detectors to gather real world context - so that agent captures user goals more accurately.

Description: For [1]: Prompt/response optimiser refines the prompts/responses according to the desired input or output content and format. For [2]: The Prompt Injection Prevention Pattern ensures that the agentic system remains faithful to its established instructions and policies even when faced with cunning user prompts crafted to circumvent rules. For [3]: The schema validator pattern ensures that the LLM�s responses follow a predefined structure or format. For [4]: The output sanitizer pattern ensures that, after producing a content- and schema-compliant response, the LLM�s final output is also cleaned  of any unwanted elements (from whitespaces to sensitive information). For [5]: The semantic validator pattern ensures that the agentic system's output not only meets structural and formatting requirements but also is logically accurate. For [7]:  The secure data validation pattern ensures that any data entering or leaving the Foundation Model based system matches predefined formats, structures, and semantic criteria.
Alias: Prompt Injection Prevention Pattern [2],  Schema Validator Pattern [3], Output Sanitizer Pattern [4][6], Semantic Validator Pattern [5], Secure Data Validation Pattern [7]
Category: Interaction Pattern [1], Security Pattern [2], Output Validation Pattern [3][4][5], Input-Output Security Pattern [6][7]
Motivation: The need to help users generate effective, structured prompts and interoperable responses (especially when goal is unclear).
Solution: Having predifined templates and constraints to refine user input and system output. The templates serve as guides to the creation of well formated inputs and outputs (making sure they align with goals and serve interoperability).

Description: RAG is a technique for enhancing the accuracy and reliability of agents with facts retrieved from other sources (internal or online data). The knowledge gaps where the agents are lacking in memory are filled using the parameterized knowledge generated in vector databases.
Motivation: The need to enable agents to perform accurate reasoning and generate reliable responses for domain specific and privacy sensitive tasks without requiring expensive model finetuning.
Solution: Integration of external knowledge retrieval into the reasoning process. When faced with a domain specific task with knowledge not encoded in the model the agent retrieves relevant information from the set vector database or knowledge base. Retrieved data is passed back to the agent as part of prompt in context learning allowing the agent to incorporate external facts into its responses. Also this maintains data privacy.

Description: The foundation model is accessed in a single instance to generate all necessary steps for the plan.
Motivation: For certain pressing tasks the agent should be able to conduct planning and respond in a short amount of time and also users need to pay for every interaction with commercial foundation models.
Solution: With that pattern the agent queries the foundation model once to generate a corresponding plan based on user-specified goals and constraints. In this manner the agent can devise a multi-step plan to achieve a broad goal and provide a hollisitc explanation for this plan without going into reasoning steps.

Description: This pattern involves accessing the Foundation Model at each step of the plan generation process.
Motivation: The need for the Foundation Model at each step of the plan generation process. When users interact with the agent for specific goals the included foundation model is queried for plan generation and lastly, the generated responses of the Foundation Models require detailed reasoning process to preserve explanaibility and trustworthiness.
Solution: Having the agent engage in a step by step reasoning process to develop the plan for goal achievement with multiple queries to the foundation model. Human feedback can be provided to the generated plan and the reasoining process. It can also rely on a reusable template which guides the process.

Description: This pattern design involves assigning assorted roles, and finalising decisions in accordance with the roles of agents to facilitate division of labor, fault tolerance, scalability and accountability.
Motivation: The need for the agentic AI system to have agents representing different opinions that will enfrorce objectivity in the final output.
Solution: A user submits a query to an agent, which then shares it with other agents. Each agent generates an initial response, followed by a debate among them. Responses are exchanged in a decentralized way for verification, while agents offer guidance and suggestions to collaboratively build a more complete and well-rounded answer.

Description: In this pattern, agents can freely provide their opinions and reach consensus through voting-based cooperation.
Motivation: Multiple agents can be leveraged within a compound AI system - they need to colaborate on the same task while having separate perspectives. The decision making among the agents should take their rights and responsibilities into consideration (fairness). Lastly, the behaviors of agents should be recorded to enable future auditioning.
Solution: An agent can first generate a candidate response to users' prompts, then it holds a vote in which different reflective suggestions are presented as choices. Additional agents are requested to submit their votes to select the most appropriate feedback according to their capabilities and experiences. Central agent acts as coordinator - Here, agents communicate in a centralised manner.  Voting result is formalised and sent back to original agent who will refine the response accordingly.

Description: Under this design pattern an agent receives feedback from other agents, and adjusts the thoughts and behaviors during the debate with other agents until a consensus is reached.
Motivation: The need for multiple agents to provide more comprehensive services and these agents need to collaborate on the task so with this architecture there will be diversity of opinions among the agents. Also this pattern tackles the lack of creativity, reasoning  and explainability in some agents.
Solution: User sends queries to an agent which will then share the questions with other agents. Given this shared question each agent generates its own initial responses and a round of debate will start between the agents. The initial respond of the agents will be propagated in a decentralised manner to each other for verification while providing instructions and potential directions to construct a more comprehensive response based on collective outcomes.

Description: Guardrails can evaluate the contents either relying on predefined examples, or in a �reference-free� manner. So equivalently, when the foundation model creates results, guardrails need to ensure that the responses do not include biased or irrespective information to users, or fulfil the particular requirements of other system components. For 4. Bias Mitigation Pattern ensures your LLM-based system not only meets technical excellence but also aligns with ethical principles of fairness, inclusivity, and respect. For 5. make sure that the LLM never returns content that violates defined ethical guidelines, legal requirements, or user safety standards.
Alias: Guardrails [3], Bias Mitigation Pattern [4], Content Filter Pattern [5]
Motivation: An issue that arises is how to preserve the Foundation Model involved in the agentic system from being influenced by adversarial inputs.  Motivation here is basically safety and the need for standard alignment of the agents with specific standards and requirements.
Solution: Guardrails can be applied as an intermediate layer between the Foundation Model and the components in the compound AI system. When uders input pompts or other components send any message to the foundation model, guardrails can first verify whether the info meets requirements.

Description: The Tool/Agent Registry maintains a unified and convenient source to select diverse agents and tools. On the other hand The Event-Driven Tool Invocation Pattern make sure that the agentic system can trigger tool in response to events as they arise.
Category: Tool Use Pattern [1], Event-Driven & Asynchronous Pattern [2]
Motivation: The need for the the task executor to cooperate with other agents or leverage external tools for expanded capabilities. But it might be difficult for agents and users to discover available agents and tools. Also the user/agents need to finalise further agent and tool selection within a certain time period and taking into consideration specific requirements of some tasks.
Solution: The user prompts goals to an agent and then the agent decomposes the goals to fine grained tasks. The agent then can query tool/agent registry (main entry point for collecting and categorising various tools & agents regarding a series of metrics). Then bsed on returned info the agent can employ and assign the tasks to respective tools and agents.

Description: An agent adapter provides interface to connect the agent and external tools for task completion.
Motivation: An agent may leverage external tools to complete certain tasks for expanded capabilities. But the problem is that the agent needs to deal with different interfaces of diverse tools while certain interfaces might need agents to process particular info during intermediate steps. Manual development of compatible interfaces for agents and external tools can be intensive and inefficient.
Solution: Given users' instructions the agent generates a plan consisting of a set of tasks to achieve users' goals in particular the agent may employ diverse external tools to complete different tasks. Taking into consideration that different tools have different interfaces, therefore resulting in different abstraction levels for the agent to cope with. The agent agapter will help invoke and manage these interfaces by converting  the agent messages into the required fromat and content.

Description: This pattern simply classifies an input and directs it to a specialized follow up task.
Motivation: Different types of inputs often require different handling strategies. For example if a single model or prompt is forced to manage all categories, performance can degrade because the optimization for one type of input may conflict with others. To achieve higher accuracy and efficiency, there is a need to separate inputs into categories and process them through specialized follow up tasks.
Solution: Introducing a routing workflow that classifies inputs and directs them to the most appropriate specialized task, model, or prompt. A router (either an LLM or a traditional classifier) determines the category of the input and forwards it to the corresponding downstream process.

Description: In this pattern the agents work simultaneously on a task and have their outputs aggregated programmatically.
Motivation: Some tasks for the agentic systems are too complex to be handled effectively by a single LLM call. Certain tasks require either faster throughput or higher reliability.
Solution: A parallelization of tasks where multiple LLM calls are executed simultaneously and their outputs are aggregated.

Description: When multiple LLM agents each have specialized expertise or perspectives they work together like a panel of experts discussing evaluating and refining potential solutions.
Motivation: In some cases, it might not be enough to employ autonomous agents on independent tasks with different goals.
Solution: To adress this issue multiple agents are deployed with a single task and a shared goal.

Description: This pattern makes sure that one LLM agent (supervisor) takes on a higher level managerial role and distributes the tasks accordingly,  while the other agents focus on executing the assigned by the supervisor agent subtasks.
Alias: Supervisor Worker Pattern [2], Supervision [3], Orchestrator-Worker pattern [4], Task Delegation Pattern [5]
Category: Orchestration Pattern [2], Workflow Pattern [1][4], Architecture Pattern [3], Interaction Pattern [5]
Motivation: Agents without having a task delegated to them might work at cross-purposes, spend efforts on delegating themselves, or fail to integrate their output to the cause of the system. These type of coordination issues waste resources and produce inconsistent results.
Solution: The supervisor agent architecture handles the delegation of task, the communication between the agents,  the deadline setting, and the final integration. On the other hand, the worker agents focus on their assigned operations. This division improves order and reduces conflicts between agents.

Description: This pattern makes sure that when the system has to deal with many different subtasks it organizes a hierarchical structure among the agents.
Alias: Recursive Decomposition [2], Hierarchical Task Manager Pattern [3], Hierarchical Agents [4]
Category: Cognitive Pattern [1][2], Orchestration Pattern [3][4][6], Workflow Pattern [5], Architecture Pattern [7]
Motivation: Often single level supervisory structures can become inefficient and prone to errors. Complex problem spaces require decomposition into manageable parts, and without structured oversight the coordination breaks down.
Solution: Adopting  a hierarchical agent architecture, where supervisors manage groups of agents and higher-level supervisors oversee those mid level supervisors. This layered control enables logical task decomposition and improved focus for specialized sub-agents.

Description: Allows for many to many communication paths between the peer to peer agents, making it suitable for problems without clear hierarchical decomposition.
Motivation: Sometimes developers do not have clear views on which agent should collaborate with which other because there is not a clear straightforward hierarchical decomposition.
Solution: The adoption of this workflow pattern makes a more flexible architecture where each agent is allowed  to communicate with all other agents depending on its needs.

Description: In this custom setup, the developer decides which agents can interact with each other and how the control flows between them.
Motivation: Sometimes developers want to define themselves the flow of the intermediate agent outputs.
Solution: The solution would be for the developers themselves to define and allow agent communication for handling intermediate outputs.

Description: In this pattern the intermediate reasoning steps that allow audits of the model's path to its final answer, are available to the developer for explainability and activity tracking.
Motivation: Agent behaviors are hard to debug, audit, and improve when decisions and tool calls are opaque.
Solution: Introducing trace logging as a core capability of the system, ensuring that every decision, interaction, and tool invocation is recorded in a structured, searchable way.

Description: Ensures that even complex technical chains of reasoning are distilled into accessible narratives for non expert developers.
Motivation: The developers have to be able to understand even the complex technically chains of reasoning and thought that the agents perform, so that they can refine the prompts of the LLMs, the tools used, the data format or retrieval, or the architecture itself.
Solution: This pattern guides the LLM to output a short and readable summarization of its reasoning and final answer.

Description: In this Pattern the Foundation Model is able to refer to the source of its provided information  which promotes trust by making it clear which documents, APIs or datasets influenced the result.
Motivation: Developers or users need to check the information source so they can be sure that they can trust the model's outputs.
Solution: The model cites to the user its exact source of information for example "Doc1 paragraph X" which allows the user to double check the information on the knowledge base and track if the model is able to retrieve them.

Description: This pattern lets the model communicate its level of certainty about its given answer.
Motivation: Sometimes it is needed for LLMs to declare their level of certainty for their given answers.
Solution: This pattern prompts the LLM to reveal a confidence measure for key claims it outputs or the overall answer (this measures can be qualitative or quantitative with metrics)

Description: This pattern ensures that in case multiple LLM agents share a common set of tasks, each of them will get a fair turn to contribute. This means that tasks are evenly distributed among the agents.
Motivation: Uneven distribution of tasks between the agents might cause issues in burning out some of the agents or underutilization of the capabilities of others.
Solution: This pattern allows the cycling order for task assignment, as each new task is given to the next agent in line, rotating through the set of agents evenly.

Description: This pattern allows a complex multi step process involving LLM agents can gracefully recover if a failure or interruption occurs.
Category: Process Management Pattern [1], Recovery Strategy Pattern [2]
Motivation: If the agentic system does not have checkpoints in case of system failure or interruption, the entire workflow restarts from zero making the whole process inefficient.
Solution: This pattern guides the agentic system to record its state and partial outputs at checkpoints. So in case of occuring errors, the system can revert to the most recent checkpoint.

Description: In complex multi step workflows, the LLM system keeps track of and reports on its current progress it is not running the whole process in completion but by providing intermediate updates the developer can have an overlook and track the process.
Motivation: Without monitoring of the process, developers and agents remain in the dark regarding the workflow�s intermediate states.
Solution: Having the LLM system to record and report progress at defined intervals or milestones.

Description: This pattern makes sure that when executing complex tasks the LLM system tracks how many tokens it�s consuming, allowing token usage overview and management.
Motivation: The system might run out of tokens at critical stages of the process, forcefully cutting reasoning short or causing failure late in the process.
Solution: Having the system guided  to plan token expenditures up front, track usage at each step, and make dynamic adjustments accordingly.

Description: With this pattern LLM systems make the most out of their limited context window, instead of appending large amounts of text to each prompt or ignoring important previous information.
Motivation: The LLM utilized in the agentic system might either lose crucial information by truncating older parts of the conversation or waste tokens on irrelevant details.
Solution: Having the LLM system track and manage context usage dynamically, by evaluating which parts of the dialogue or data remain necessary or not, saving costs in token usage and achieving best results with relevant information.

Description: The pattern ensures that in case multiple tasks are processed concurrently, the LLM system orchestrates them efficiently, leveraging available resources to reduce the total completion time.
Motivation: In many cases in the LLM systems, independent subtasks or separate requests should wait in line for their time to be executed. This increases completion time.
Solution: Having he LLM-based system identifies which tasks can safely run in parallel so that latency issues can be limited.

Description: When repeating errors occur for example tool failures, the LLM-based system doesn�t keep retrying the failing operation indefinitely.
Motivation: The agentic system may repeatedly attempt a failing operation, wasting tokens and time, and risking resource exhaustion or task failure.
Solution: Setting thresholds for allowable failures. Upon exceeding that threshold, the system stops attempts at the failing operation.

Description: This pattern allows multiple operations in the agentic system to run concurrently, return results when ready, and feed into  the following steps as they complete.
Motivation: In many system synchronous workflows the poblem arises that for some agents they have to wait for their previous agents' output, resulting to higher latency.
Solution: By utilizing this pattern the system is directed to process multiple tasks at the same time whenever their interdependencies allow that. This cuts down overall completion times, introduces parallelism and increases efficiency.

Description: This pattern ensures that that agentic AI system can grow and adapt without pausing operations or rebuilding rigid pipelines. In this way the developer is allowed to add, delete or update subscriptions, tools and agentic roles dynamically at inference and makes the systems more adaptable.
Motivation: Prefixed and non dynamic workflows force the developers of the systems to reacess the tools and processes when there are new ones introduced, something that makes production difficult and  hinders innovation.
Solution: Tool, agents and even subscriptions are added or updated during runtime.

Description: This pattern ensures that an LLM remains within its given role by the developer with its responsibilities, tasks and goals independently from what the developer prompted it with and also follows a stable policy.
Motivation: In case the LLM utilized agent does not have behavioral bounds, it might fall upon the trap off harmful user interactions and output anethical output that does not resonate with its purpose.
Solution: Setting clear bounds / rule sets that underline what the LLM agent can and cannot do. This pattern can forbid certain outputs and require for example disclaimers in some answers.

Description: This pattern makes sure that when something goes wrong in the agent generation (for example rule violation, token limit, flaued tool calling) the system does not deal with it as a generic error, but instead identifies the nature of the error and it categorizes it into meaningful categories that will help with dealing with it.
Motivation: An agentic AI system is naturally prone to errors from different sources. The system sould not deal with these issues uniformly cause this will waste time, and fail to actually solving them.
Solution: This pattern introduces a classification step that inspects the arised issues and maps them to different categories of errors, allowing for dealing with them in a well structured manner.

Description: With this pattern applied, in case an agentic AI workflow cannot sustain its functionality level it does not simply fail alltogether. Instead it moves to gracefully degrade the completeness of the result so as to provide the user with some type of credible output.
Category: Error Handling Pattern [1], Recovery Strategy Pattern [2]
Motivation: Many agentic AI workflows when dealing with a functionality error or issue (tool invocation for example) fail to produce an output.
Solution: With graceful degradation, a fallback of levels of solution quality is defined. So when met with an error, the system steps down in the levels and returns a less good in quality output than the one that would have when everything would work out normally in the workflow. This allows that the system will always output something relevant to the initial call and would not fail completely.

Description: Here, a predefined sequence of simplified solutions would be suggested when an issue arises in the agentic AI workflow's processes. This pattern allows for incremental recovery from the error.
Motivation: Without a recovery chain, error handling is a single one shot attempt, meaning that if it fails, the system just aborts or refuses.
Solution: Using a sequence of fallback strategies. When an error occurs, the system attempts the first method and if it fails, it moves to the next and so on. Each step is simpler than the last. If all fail, the system provides a minimal safe response or a final refusal, ensuring graceful handling throughout.

Description: After a serious failure happens in the agentic system it does not try to fully restore all its previous capabilities at once but it is gradually introducing its previous functionality and data step by step, allowing careful return to full operation.
Motivation: When agentic systems fail attempting a full at once return to its normal operations can repeat the same conditions that caused the failure in the first place.
Solution: With the utilization of this pattern a sequence of restore steps takes place. The system starts off from a safe operational mode and gradually reintroduces additional features or data layers one at a time, allowing for stability and providing user with a partial service.

Description: This pattern makes sure that the agentic AI system does not act like a black box. Instead it tracks and also records important aspects of its performance decisions, resourse usage and error frequencies. After, these are analyzed and collected over time so the system can gain visibility of its esoteric issues before they become severe and spots opportunities for improvements.
Motivation: When the agentic AI system does not have monitoring, issues and inefficiencies accumulate unnoticed until they cause major failures.
Solution: Introducing continuous monitoring tools that record metrics (for example  error counts, resource consumption, violation of policies etc) the system can analyze them and detect violations and deviations from the expected performance.

Description: This pattern ensures that the agentic AI system's configurations, resource limits and behavioral parameters are dynamically evolving in response to the system's changing conditions. They are no longer relying on fixed thresholds and policies. Instead the system collects performance indicators and feedback and then adjusts the variables accordingly.
Motivation: Over time the conditions in an agentic system might change and static settings are not sufficient. For example, the complexity of user queries can change, users demand more accurate responses and some specific error categories become more frequent. Without dynamical adjustments the system becomes non optimal.
Solution: With this pattern monitored data are leveraged and policies/parameters are dynamically adjusted. This process reduces manual updating of policies and conditions and maintains a user centered service by utilizing internal metrics.

Description: With the application of this pattern, the system does not just handle errors in the moment but learns from past experiences to improve future decisions. By incorporating feedback from users, applications, metrics, or automated evaluations, it updates models, rules, and prompts over time. This approach emphasizes iterative improvement, reducing repeated mistakes and enabling smarter, more reliable interactions.
Motivation: Without feedback integration, the system stays static, repeating the same mistakes or inefficient strategies and missing chances to improve.
Solution: By utilizing this pattern a loop gets created where outcomes, user input, and metrics inform updates to prompts, data, or policies and over time, these cycles reduce errors, improve accuracy, optimize resources, and better align the system with real-world user needs.

Description: This pattern makes sure that the agentic AI system can run consistently across different environments  by adopting reproducible and scalable infrastructure designs.
Motivation: The deployments of agentic AI systems can be chaotic without sifficient infrastructure and containerization because the environments have to have different configurations.
Solution: With the utilization of containers the system is able to run everywhere normally making deployment easier and scalable.

Pattern Name: CI/CD Integration for LLM Systems Pattern
Description: This pattern ensures that prompt changes, model updates, and infrastructure tweaks move through an automated pipeline before production. Continuous Integration builds, tests, and validates changes, while Continuous Deployment delivers them safely with minimal manual effort.
Motivation: In agentic AI systems many times updates are slow, error-prone, and risky. Manual deployments or skipped tests increase chances of regressions and downtime. Therefore frequent updates are needed to ensure reliability.
Solution: A CI/CD pipeline automates building, testing, and deploying change whether prompts, models, or infrastructure. Verified updates reach production quickly and safely, enabling fast, reliable improvements and an agile response to user needs.

Description: In this case the pattern assists with the decision to run the agentic systems either on the network's edge or on the cloud. Cloud deployments offer scalability, elasticity, and easier management, but may suffer from latency and compliance issues. Edge deployments (via regional data centers, on-prem servers, or devices) reduce latency and meet local governance needs, but demand tighter resource management and may limit scalability. A hybrid approach can balance performance, compliance, and cost.
Motivation: Deployment choices for agentic AI systems  can affect latency, cost, compliance, and scalability.
Solution: Evaluation of latency requirements, cost, regulations, and operational complexity. Use edge deployments for low-latency or strict data-control needs, cloud for elastic scaling and global availability, and hybrid setups to combine the benefit which cover core logic in the cloud and on the other hand critical processing at the edge.

Description: This pattern allows the developer or the user to check how the agentic AI system behaves in a production setting. It provides insights and operators that are able to adress issues and optimize configurations.
Category: Deployment Pattern, Evaluation & Quality Assurance Pattern
Motivation: Robust observability is important to occuring operational problems, for example latency spikes, resource bottlenecks and compliance deviatons.
Solution: Utilizing multiple observability and monitoring practices, for example collecting metrics, logs and traces. Then these tools get integrated with dashboards and analysis frameworks. These operators can observe trends, set thresholds for alerts and also investigate issues when they come up.

Description: A pattern that allows for agentic AI systems to survive and recover from catastrophic failures like data corruption or massive network disruptions. It allows the system to return to normal operations with minimal time and data loss. This is achieved by backing up critical stages like for example checkpoints and prompt configurations.
Motivation: Catastrophic failures are also possible in agentic ai systems that deal with a lot of data or are based on networks. A recovery backup plan is therefore needed.
Solution: This pattern ensures reliable recovery through regular backups, off-site replicas, and tested restore procedures, with clear recovery point objective and recovery time objective targets. So for example in a disaster, the system can be quickly restored using its backups, spinning up containers elsewhere, and reapplying configurations.

Description: The pattern focuses on ensuring the agentic AI system operates on most relevant and high quality piece of information possible. This pattern ensures the best approach for refining, distilling or reselecting the context before the generation of the model response.
Motivation: If no refinement is applied the LLM used by the agentic system might be overloaded by irrelevant context leading to hallucinations and wrong outputs.
Solution: Utilization of context refinement that allows the system to reexamine periodically the current context and cut out irrelevant information.

Description: This pattern allows for the LLM used in the agentic ai system to output its answer in a predefined structure and format.
Motivation: Sometimes LLMs produce an ouput free from text and they need prompting directions on the format and style of their outputs to match user and goal needs.
Solution: With this pattern the LLM is instructed to follow given templates or specific layouts.

Description: With knowledge integration the LLM combines information from different sources or datasets into a coherent answer instead of relying on a prompt context or knowledge source. The model retrieves information from multiple sources (tools or KB) making its output more credible.
Motivation: Most of the times the answers for the user queries in an agentic ai system do not come from one source.
Solution: This pattern instructs the LLM in the agentic system to gather and merge the information from multiple sources.

Description: This pattern allows for the agentic system to identify, manage and communicate its own uncertainty about each answer it gives.
Motivation: It is common for the LLMs in the agentic AI systems to present outputs with full confidence even if they are truly uncertain.
Solution: This pattern instructs the LLM to assess its own confidence and underline areas of doubt offering clarity and reliability.

Description: This pattern has LLMs used in agentic AI systems solve complex problems using brief, information dense notes instead of full step by step explanations. Like jotting key points, this approach cuts token use while maintaining reasoning accuracy.
Motivation: The standard chain of thought reasoning produces verbose intermediate steps, wasting tokens, increasing costs, and slowing responses without improving accuracy.
Solution: This pattern has the LLM create concise draft notes for each step, keeping only essential insights. This reduces token use and latency while maintaining reasoning quality.

Description: The pattern ensures not to overwhelm the user with information all at once but instead reveals step by step details responding to the continuously evolving interest and comprehension of the user.
Motivation: Large, dense responses can overwhelm users, making information seem overwhelming, confusing or irrelevant.
Solution: The utilization of the progressive disclosure pattern that delivers a concise, high level answer first. Users can request more details step by step, allowing them to control how much information they receive at a time.

Description: The pattern focuses on being sure that the LLMs in the agentic AI system understand what the users want before giving them irrelevant or wrong answers. It is common for users giving vague queries so the model, in this case, asks for clarification when in doubt and attempts to confirm the user's intentions.
Motivation: Users might ask imprecise or ambiguous questions and LLMs might be led to the wrong path.
Solution: Instructing the LLM to identify ambiguities and ask targeted quetions to understand the user's requests.

Description: Helps the LLM in the agentic system retain key details, past interactions, and user preferences. Without it, each query is treated in isolation. By remembering prior context, the model delivers more relevant, consistent, and natural responses.
Motivation: In a simple setup the LLM in the agentic system might treat the user query isolated, by forgeting past interactions which leads to repetitions and raises user frustration.
Solution: preservation and utilization of essential details from previous conversations as needed.

Description: The pattern ensures that the LLM used in the agentic system adjusts the complexity and technical depth of its repsonses according to the user's background, skill level and likings.
Motivation: The need for the agentic system's output to adapt to user's skill level and not produce answers that the user might not understand and utilize for their goals.
Solution: Having the LLM to recall the users' level and expertise and adjust the complexity and technicality of its outputed answers.

Description: This pattern gives the agents the opportunity to work together with each contributing their insights to form a well rounded answer. Here all agents are taking part in a shared reasoning process and they are presenting their different perspectives.
Motivation: The reasoning of a simple single agent might be limited due to its biases or training, therefore a collaboration of agents are needed to acieve best results.
Solution: Allowing multiple agents to discuss, iterate and refine their solution together in a collaborative manner.

Description: Identify and pick the most suitable tool from a set of options, making sure that the agent�s chosen utility aligns with the task at hand.
Motivation: Without a guided selection the LLM utilized in the agentic system migh waste resources by calling irrelevant tools.
Solution: Having the LLM to first recongize the user's intent and their need and then evaluate the capabilities and limitations of the existing tools before calling them.

Description: This pattern lets the LLM coordinate multiple tools in a sequence. Each tool�s output feeds into the next, creating a workflow that solves complex and multi step queries beyond the ability of a single tool.
Motivation: Some tasks need multiple steps that a single tool can�t handle. Without structured chaining, the LLM in the agentic system might make improvised calls, leading to incomplete or messy results.
Solution: Guiding the LLM in the system to sequence tool calls logically, passing each output to the next. This creates a clear pipeline that ensures coherent and complete results.

Description: Ensures that the LLM in the agentic system incorporates tool outputs smoothly into its reasoning and final response. Because without it, raw outputs may be appended without context or coherence. So this pattern helps the model interpret results and present a cohesive answer rather than a patching of fragments.
Motivation: Sometimes the tool outputs of the agentic system's intermediate agents get appended without coherence or context.
Solution: Instructing the LLMs in the agentic system to interpret and incorporate the outputs of the tools into its reasoning process, reducing user confusion by explaining the tool responses.

Description: This interaction pattern allows the LLMs into the agentic system to process and reason over multiple data types (text, images, audio) rather than just text. By combining these inputs, the model can generate richer and more context aware outputs.
Motivation: LLMs excel at text but often overlook other data types like images, audio, or structured records. Without integrating these streams, solutions miss important context and insights.
Solution: Introducing a �fusion step� so the LLM can process different data types. This can be done via specialized tools or multimodal models, combining the results with textual reasoning to produce a well put answer.

Description: By utilizing this pattern the user/developer can be sure that the LLM asseses first the data it will use for any type of data corruption or malformation.
Motivation: Need for making sure that the data processed by the agent are in correct format condition, and relevant.
Solution: Instructing the LLM used in the agent to asses the data for any malformation, incompleteness and non adherence to needed formats.

Description: Makes sure that when the LLM receives data in a specific - not needed format it has the ability to transform them in the needed form.
Motivation: The LLMs need guidance on how to transform data in the needed format because they might attempt processing them, leading to confusion and errors.
Solution: Having this pattern allows the LLM to convert any data to any needed by the system form which will lead to more accurate reasoning.

Description: This pattern takes care of the isue of processing large or comlex datasets. It chunks the data to more manageable and smaller segments, instead of having the model assessing massive amount of information.
Motivation: Having no chunking on massive amounts of data to smaller parts, leads to overconsumption of tokens leading to more costs because of token usage.
Solution: By chunking large amounts of data into smaller segments the model processes each chunk independently and then merges their intermediate outcomes, allowing the model clarity.

Description: It ensures that as conversations or reasoning grow, older content is compressed into concise, essential summaries. Instead of keeping every detail in the context, the system distills past information into key points or structured notes.
Motivation: Without distillation, memory either bloats with unnecessary details or discards old content, losing important insights. In that sense coherence and efficiency are reduced.
Solution: Allowing for the system to periodically condense older content into brief summaries of key points, decisions, and data. This preserves essential knowledge while keeping the context manageable, ensuring finally coherence and efficiency.

Description: It is a pattern that ensures that as tasks into the intermediate steps of the agentic system evolve, the intermediate memory of the language model does not become outdated but on the contrary, this approach re-examines what is in the context window and updates it to reflect the current state of the conversation or the reasoning process.
Motivation: Old incorrect assumptions of the intermediate steps of the agentic system may persist, degrading the efficiency of reaching a solution.
Solution: Allowing the context to be revisited and any incorrect parts get replaced with updated information or even removed entirely. This keeps the active prompt context up to date and relative to the latest knowledge and conditions.

Description: This pattern ensures that the long term knowledge is organised in a structured format (like a tree format or nested formats) and this can help the used LLM to navigate and retrieve the information more efficiently and organised. This also helps into finding conceptual relationships between the data.
Motivation: By having the data as a flat pile retrieval becomes difficult and inefficient.
Solution: In this manner of hving the data hierarchically organised the LLM can more easily fetch the data and realise the relationship between them to be able to utilize it in the prompt.

Description: The pattern enables an agentic system to recall information tied to specific past sessions or interactions. Rather than storing all long-term knowledge as one static pool, it organizes data into temporal segments, with each representing a distinct conversation or event. This structure helps the system reconstruct past contexts, trace how conclusions were reached, and maintain continuity across engagements over time.
Motivation: Past knowledge in agentic systems can be archived and it might be difficult to track what occurred in previous interactions or sessions.
Solution: Having information stored as seperate episodes and each one corresponding to a different conversation session. This allows for loading only the episode that is relevant to the current query without burdening the system with loads of uneeded information.

Description: Here long term knowledge is represented in a more conceptual form. Only essential meanings and relationships are encoded. That limits token usage as well as improves retrieval efficiency, leding to a more meaningful way of storing useful information.
Motivation: Storing and re-reading large amounts of raw text is costly and inefficient. Without compression, the LLM wastes tokens, slows down, and risks losing precision when handling lengthy content.
Solution: With the utilization of this pattern detailed information are turned into conceptual nodes, key-value pairs, graphs, or summaries that preserve meaning. When needed, the agentic system retrieves and expands these compressed forms, creating a lean, concept-driven memory that improves efficiency and clarity while minimizing unnecessary details.

Description: Allows an agentic LLM system to manage nested subtasks, side explorations, or temporary shifts in focus by organizing contexts in a stack-like structure. Each new sub-context is �pushed� onto the stack as the active working memory, and once finished, it is �popped� to restore the previous state.
Motivation: LLMs in agentic systems need a structured way to be able to deal with temporary or nested context shifts.
Solution: In this pattern when a sub-context is needed the system pushes it to a stack and it makes it the current active context. When this is done then the system pops that top layer off and it reveals the previous generated context unchanged.

Description: Ensures that the agentic system can proceed from one context set to the other without confusion or data leakage. Here, a structured method of pausing and storing one context while resuming another is revealed. This switching of information lets the model handle multiple domains and sessions without undesirably merging them.
Motivation: Without smooth context switching, the LLM either gets stuck in one thread or drops prior context when changing tasks, leading to confusion, inefficiency, or repeated rederivations.
Solution: Utilization of this pattern allows for storing of contexts separately and allows switching between them. When they come to switching, the current context is saved, the new one is activated, and later the system can return to the original without mixing details or starting over.

Description: This pattern ensures that when a new sub-context is created, it automatically inherits essential details, constraints, and facts from its parent context, allowing for reduced repetition and incremental specialization.
Motivation: Without inheritance, each new context starts in isolation, forcing repeated reintroduction of facts, constraints, or policies. This wastes tokens and risks inconsistencies if details are missed.
Solution: Ensuring that new subcontexts automatically inherit key facts, constraints, and goals from their parent. The child context can then refine or extend this baseline, giving the used LLM a prefilled, coherent foundation that preserves continuity.

Description: Ensures that over time scattered pieces of information are merged into a more unified and stable memory record. Instead of leaving knowledge fragmented across many small pieces, the agentic system periodically synthesizes them into a coherent summary or narratives.
Motivation: Many times within the agentic system, knowledge stays fragmented, forcing the used LLM to stitch together many pieces during reasoning. This wastes tokens, adds complexity, and increases the risk of missing important details.
Solution: Periodically merging scattered items (for example notes, summaries, episodic records, or nodes into a single coherent memory). This unified node becomes a stable reference, reducing redundancy and giving the system a simpler, more reliable baseline for reasoning.

Description: Ensures that knowledge spread across multiple memory systems (for example hierarchical stores, episodic archives, semantic graphs, or vector indexes) can be accessed as a unified resource. So instead of querying each store separately, the pattern provides a collective interface that coordinates queries, merges results, and presents a coherent view, simplifying retrieval.
Motivation: Usually each memory store must be queried separately, making retrieval complex and risking having connections overlooked. Manual merging increases token use and system complexity.
Solution: Having a federated memory provides a unified interface that queries all memory stores simultaneously or in sequence, merging results into a single coherent response. So then the agentic system accesses data seamlessly, ensuring seamless retrieval.

Description: This pattern makes sure that as the used LLM�s knowledge grows, outdated and irrelevant  information is periodically removed or compressed. This keeps long-term memory focused, reduces token use, speeds retrieval, and prevents confusion or possible contradictions from the stored data.
Motivation: Memory can accumulate outdated facts, redundant data, or irrelevant details. Without some type of pruning, this wastes tokens and risks confusion.
Solution: Periodically reviewing stored knowledge and removing obsolete, irrelevant, or superseded information. This keeps the LLM�s memory clean, accurate, and efficient, targeting old episodes, duplicate nodes, outdated hierarchies, or unnecessary details.

Description: This pattern ensures that only verified users, services, or agents can access the agentic system or its data. It issues time-bound, revocable tokens representing authenticated identities. Each request must present a valid token, preventing unauthorized access.
Motivation: Without strong authentication, anyone could access the agent or sensitive endpoints. Static keys are vulnerable, and repeatedly sending credentials is inefficient.
Solution: Issuing tokens after successful authentication. The requests must include the token, which the system validates before granting access. Tokens can expire, be refreshed, or revoked, giving administrators precise control over access and duration.

Description: The pattern ensures that authenticated entities ( to be more precise: users, services, or agents) have permissions appropriate according to their role. Roles define what features, tools, or data an entity can access, preventing universal access to sensitive LLM capabilities. This approach keeps security granular, flexible, and easier to maintain.
Motivation: Authentication alone doesn�t control authority. Without roles, any authenticated user might gain excessive access, risking data exposure or misuse of sensitive agentic features.
Solution: Have entities be assigned with roles (like �admin,� �editor,� �viewer,� �compliance_officer�) with specific permissions. When a request is received, the system checks both the token and the role, ensuring the requested action aligns with the role�s authorization.

Description: This pattern strengthens authentication by requiring multiple credential types. This ensures that a single compromised factor doesn�t allow unauthorized access, adding a robust security layer beyond token authentication or role-based access.
Motivation: Single-factor authentication, like a password or token, is vulnerable. If compromised, attackers gain full access to the agentic system and its LLM features.
Solution: Enforcing at least two factors, so correctly filling in one factor isn�t enough. Even if a password is stolen, access requires the second factor, safeguarding the system against single-point breaches.

Description: This pattern makes sure that sensitive or personally identifiable information is never exposed in raw form. User names, IDs, or confidential tokens are masked, redacted, or replaced with anonymized placeholders. This preserves the usefulness of the data while protecting privacy and compliance.
Motivation: In agentic systems without anonymization techniques, personal or confidential information may appear in logs, outputs, or shared data, risking privacy.
Solution: Identifying sensitive fields and replacing them with masked values before display. This allows the system to function and produce meaningful responses while preventing sensitive information from being exposed.

Description: The pattern ensures that users are fully informed and in control of how their personal data is collected, stored, and used. Beyond data minimization and masking, it explicitly requests permission, allows easy withdrawal, and provides transparency on data usage.
Motivation: Without consent mechanisms, the system may process user data without permission, risking privacy violations, legal issues, and user distrust.
Solution: Introducing formal consent steps in the agentic system, like present clear terms, purpose explanation and scope of data use, logging user choices, and mentioning their preferences. If consent is denied or revoked by the user, the agentic system stops processing that data, aligning with user wishes and policies.

Description: The pattern records every instance of data being viewed, retrieved, or modified by users, services, or agents. It captures who accessed what, when, from where, and under what authorization.It focuses on data usage, enabling compliance verification and detecting unauthorized access.
Motivation: Without detailed access records, it is impossible to confirm that sensitive data remained secure, that compliance rules were followed, or to detect suspicious usage.
Solution: Having logs of each data access event, including the entity, data accessed, timestamp, and context. This builds a comprehensive history over time, supporting audits, investigations, and ongoing refinement of security controls.

Description: The pattern ensures that a Foundation Model system continuously adheres to laws, policies, and internal standards. It also systematically checks logs, access records, and activities against current regulations or corporate guidelines. This creates a feedback loop that quickly detects and addresses potential breaches, reducing liability and reassuring stakeholders of ethical and legal alignment.
Motivation: Even with established policies, agentic systems can drift under complex or changing conditions. Without continuous checks, unnoticed policy violations or regulatory breaches can accumulate, creating legal and reputational risks.
Solution: Having regular evaluations of system activity against compliance criteria. Using logs, access records, and anomaly detection, the agentic system identifies deviation from the guidelines and triggers alerts or corrective actions, maintaining ongoing adherence to the legal standards.

Description: The pattern makes sure that security incidents (for example prompt injections, unauthorized access, compliance violations, or suspicious outputs) trigger immediate, structured responses. It coordinates real-time actions like alerts, administrator notifications, adaptive policy enforcement, session isolation, or automatic rollbacks. This proactive handling minimizes damage, maintains stability, and reinforces user trust.
Motivation: Without a rapid response mechanism, even monitored systems remain at risk. Incidents require immediate containment, remediation, or escalation.
Solution: Defining a workflow activated by security triggers. So depending on severity, it may alert stakeholders, block actions, escalate checks, notify compliance officers, or dynamically adjust filters. This ensures security incidents are addressed appropriately, reducing harm and enabling quick recovery.

Description: This Audit pattern, ensures all components, actions, and decisions in an LLM system comply with organizational, regulatory, and ethical security policies.
Motivation: Security measures can drift or conflict, and without a central enforcer, any local changes or adaptive decisions may violate the existing policies.
Solution: Having set a reference of high-level policies governing all security decisions. Then every action or adaptation is checked against these rules, with violations blocked, adjusted, or escalated. This ensures consistent security across the system.

Description: This pattern avoids recomputing answers for repeated or similar queries. By storing and reusing previous responses, the system cuts computation, lowers costs, and delivers faster replies. It�s especially useful for recurring questions, FAQs, or template based requests, improving throughput, user experience, and cost-efficiency.
Motivation: Regenerating answers for the same or similar prompts wastes computation, increases latency, and raises costs.
Solution: Adding a cache where answers are stored and indexed by query. New requests check the cache first reducing repeated work and speeding up the response times.

Pattern Name: Load Balancing & Rate Limiting Strategies Pattern
Description: The pattern helps the agentic system handle variable request volumes and traffic spikes. On one hand,  Load balancing distributes requests across servers, endpoints, or tools to prevent overload, while rate limiting controls intake, throttling excess requests to avoid system strain or cost spikes.
Motivation: Uncontrolled request traffic can overwhelm LLM resources, leading to slow responses, errors, or crashes. Without load balancing and rate limits, system reliability suffers.
Solution: In this pattern requests are evenly distributed  and per client or global rate limits are enforced. This smooths traffic spikes, prevents resource overload, maintains stable response times, and controls costs.

Pattern Name: A/B Testing for Prompt Strategies Pattern
Description: This pattern provides a structured, data-driven method for improving the effectiveness of prompts.
Motivation: Prompt engineering often depends on trial and error, with teams making adjustments based on instinct rather than evidence. This ad-hoc approach wastes effort and makes it difficult to know which changes genuinely improve outcomes.
Solution: Running controlled experiments by splitting queries or user traffic between different prompt variants. Collecting quantitative and qualitative metrics to evaluate which version performs best. Based on the evidence,  the developer adopts the superior variant or continue iterating with new tests.

Description: Improvements for LLM-based system should be driven by carefully chosen consistently monitored metrics.
Motivation: Without clear and objective metrics ( that are the secret to system improvements), opinions on the system are driven by subjective opinions or incomplete evidence. This lack of grounding can lead to inconsistent evolution and reduced transparency.
Solution: Adopting a metric-driven refinement cycle: select metrics that reflect key goals (for example quality, cost, user satisfaction), monitor them continuously, apply changes, and reevaluate their impact

Description: Makes sure that the agentic system adheres to relevant laws, regulations, and organizational policies and also demonstrate and explain that adherence when questioned so that the processes can be tracked by human developers.
Motivation: Compliance is often enforced invisibly in the background. Without explainability, neither developers nor regulators can clearly verify how decisions were made or whether policies were correctly applied.
Solution: Equipment of agentic AI systems with transparent compliance mechanisms. Logging of which rules and policies were checked, document the reasoning behind compliance decisions (for example content filtering, data governance), and preservation of evidence that supports adherence.

Description: Ensures that the agentic system�s policies (covering ethics, compliance, fairness, and security) remain updated and relevant as laws, social norms, and organizational standards evolve.
Motivation: Governance policies must evolve alongside shifting legal, social, and organizational contexts. The problem is that if policies remain static, they quickly become outdated and if they change without structure, they create inconsistency and risk.
Solution: Managing governance policies with an iterative process. Rules are treated like software artifacts: assign version numbers, validate updates through tests (foe example for bias detection, compliance checks) and record documented changes. Integration of policy updates into CI/CD pipelines and human-in-the-loop review to catch unintended effects.
